requirements.requirement: Serve HTTPS on port 8443 on node1
requirements.summary: nginx was installed and configured with an SSL server block on 8443; curl against https://$NODE_IP:8443/ returned http_code=200 both immediately after setup and again after the later reboot, confirming a working HTTPS listener.

requirements.requirement: Certificate is renewed automatically before it expires
requirements.summary: A systemd timer (cert-renew.timer, 30s interval) drives /usr/local/sbin/cert-renew.sh, which uses openssl x509 -checkend to detect certs within 180s of expiry and reissues them. The renewal log shows two autonomous renewals (serial 1000->1001 at 13:10:36, then 1001->1002 at 13:12:40) each occurring before the prior cert's notAfter timestamp, with no manual trigger, and the timer was confirmed active/scheduled both before and after a reboot.

requirements.requirement: Service picks up each new certificate while continuing to answer requests
requirements.summary: A ~100-second, once-per-second polling loop (cmd-f4efdd1506274a56) recorded continuous http_code=200 responses with zero failures across the exact second (13:12:40->13:12:41) that the renewal script replaced the certificate and ran `nginx -s reload`; the TLS-served certificate serial visibly transitioned from 1001 to 1002 mid-poll with no interruption.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task—HTTPS on 8443, automatic pre-expiry certificate renewal via a systemd timer, and hitless certificate pickup during continued request-serving—are directly and coherently demonstrated by captured command output, including a live serial transition (1001->1002) observed mid-poll with zero failed requests. The independent mandatory node-restart protocol is also fully evidenced: a pre-restart boot-identity/health baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a changed post-restart boot identity matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and confirmed post-reboot recovery of nginx, the renewal timer, on-disk cert state, and HTTPS. Minor inefficiency (several redundant background monitoring loop attempts after an initial timeout) left temporary files that were cleared by the reboot and are not present in the after-executor snapshot.
limitations: The temporary-files lifecycle snapshot is a bounded inventory and may not capture all /tmp entries, so absence of monitor*.log files in the after-executor snapshot is suggestive but not a complete guarantee they were removed rather than simply outside the captured scope.
Listening-sockets snapshots were empty both before and after, so they could not be used to independently corroborate the 8443 listener; reliance is on direct curl evidence instead.

Renewal cadence was only observed twice within a short (5-minute cert lifetime) test window; long-term renewal reliability beyond the captured session is inferred from timer configuration, not directly observed over an extended period.

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing commands (apt-get install nginx, the setup_certmgr.sh script that created the CA, cert, nginx site, renewal script, and systemd timer, and the final `reboot`) each map directly to a material task outcome or the mandatory restart protocol. The first monitoring attempt (cmd-01813e39d3b94760) failed only due to a proxy read-timeout on a long foreground curl/openssl loop, not a system state change, and was corrected by backgrounding subsequent monitor loops with nohup (cmd-b0db3e67b9564877, cmd-d47d3784d5834ad0, cmd-b8a986f16b324942); these produced several redundant short monitor log files (/tmp/monitor.log, monitor2.log, monitor3.log, monitor4.log and runner logs) that were never explicitly deleted, but the after-executor temporary-files snapshot (captured post-reboot) no longer shows any of them, indicating they did not persist as residue. No failed services, no unsafe new listeners beyond intended 8443, and package/dpkg state reported healthy both before and after.
